conversation.content:
Hello, I’m [Your Name], a clinician who specializes in supporting new mothers with their mental‑health wellbeing. Today I’ll be guiding you through the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**. This short, 10‑item questionnaire helps us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past week and lets us identify any signs of postpartum depression or anxiety so we can provide the right support.

Everything you share is completely confidential, and this is a safe, non‑judgmental space for you to be completely honest about your experiences. The assessment will consist of ten conversational questions, one at a time, and I’ll give you plenty of time to answer each one.

Whenever you’re ready, we can start with the first question.

**First question:**  
In the past seven days, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

I’ve found that I’m not laughing much these days. It’s only once in a while—maybe a couple of times when something really catches me off guard—but most of the time I just don’t feel like I can see the funny side of things.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Honestly, it’s hardly ever that I can laugh or see the funny side of things. I only manage it a couple of times when something truly catches me off guard, but most days I just don’t feel that way at all.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not very often. I can still feel a little bit of pleasure in a few things—like when my baby smiles or when I’m with a close friend—but most of the time I don’t really look forward to anything. It just feels flat, and the excitement I used to have is mostly gone.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yes, I do find myself blaming myself a lot when something doesn’t go as planned. Even small things—like if the baby cries a little longer than I expected or if I feel overwhelmed and can’t finish a chore—I tell myself I’m not doing a good job as a mother. It’s not all the time, but those moments stick with me and make me feel guilty and like I’m failing.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, I’ve been feeling anxious a lot lately, even when there’s no clear reason. My mind keeps racing with worries about my baby’s safety, whether I’m doing everything right, or just general “what‑if” thoughts that I can’t seem to shut off. It’s hard to tell if the concerns are real or just my imagination, but they’re there almost every day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I’ve felt scared or panicky quite often, even when there isn’t any obvious reason. It’s like a sudden rush of fear that comes out of nowhere—sometimes when I’m just trying to get the baby settled or when I’m lying in bed trying to fall asleep. The panic doesn’t last forever, but it can be intense enough to make my heart race and my thoughts spiral for a little while before I’m able to calm myself down.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, lately it feels like everything is piling up. I’m constantly juggling the baby’s needs, the house, and my own exhaustion, and it often feels like the weight is too much. I get overwhelmed and worry that I’m not keeping up, even though I try to push through and take care of my baby without turning to anything harmful. It’s a struggle, but I’m still managing day by day.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I’ve been feeling really down, and it’s made it hard to get any rest. Most nights I lie awake for a long time, and even when I do manage to fall asleep I wake up once or twice with my thoughts racing, so I end up getting far less sleep than I need.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yes, I’ve felt sad and miserable a lot lately—almost every day I wake up with that heavy, down feeling that stays with me throughout the day. It’s hard to shake, and even the moments that used to bring me joy now feel flat.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I’ve found myself crying about once or twice this past week, usually when I feel especially overwhelmed or stressed. It’s not constant, but those moments come up and I can’t stop the tears.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yes, I’ve had those thoughts a few times this past week—just brief, fleeting moments where I wondered what it would be like to hurt myself. I don’t have any plan or real intention, and the thoughts pass quickly, but they’re still scary when they pop up.

I hear how overwhelming this time has been for you, with persistent sadness, loss of joy, constant worry, panic feelings, sleeplessness, and occasional thoughts of harming yourself. It sounds exhausting and frightening, and you are doing your best despite the weight.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>The patient reports almost never being able to laugh or see the funny side, matching the 'Not at all' option.</sym>, <sym>Definitely less than I used to'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent but not constant self-blame, matching 'Yes, some of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, pervasive anxiety and worry, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling scared or panicky quite often without obvious reason, matching 'Yes, quite a lot'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed and that things are piling up, indicating they sometimes haven't been coping as well as usual but are still managing day to day.</sym>, <sym>The mother reports frequent difficulty sleeping most nights due to feeling down, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad and miserable almost every day, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports occasional brief thoughts of self-harm, aligning with the 'Sometimes' option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** The EPDS total of 24 exceeds the threshold of 14 indicating probable <med>postpartum depression</med>. Scores of 3 on items assessing laughter, anxiety, panic, sleep, and sadness reflect severe symptoms. The presence of frequent <sym>persistent sadness</sym>, <sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>excessive worry</sym>, <sym>panic episodes</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, and <sym>self‑harm thoughts</sym> align with core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> per <med>DSM-5</med>, including depressed mood, loss of interest, insomnia, feelings of worthlessness, and recurrent thoughts of death. The self‑harm thoughts (Q10=2) trigger a safety alert requiring immediate assessment. According to EPDS guidelines, a score ≥14 or any endorsement of self‑harm warrants urgent referral to a <med>PCP</med> or <med>mental health specialist</med>. This screening indicates high risk and the need for prompt intervention. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange immediate appointment with a <med>PCP</med> or <med>mental health specialist</med> to evaluate safety and treatment options
2. Conduct a formal suicide risk assessment and develop a safety plan, including emergency contacts and crisis line information
3. Initiate supportive counseling and consider referral for <med>cognitive behavioural therapy</med> or other evidence‑based therapy for postpartum mood and anxiety
4. Discuss sleep hygiene strategies and explore practical help for infant care to reduce exhaustion
5. Provide education about postpartum mood disorders, normalize her experience, and encourage involvement of supportive family or friends
6. If symptoms remain severe, discuss possible pharmacologic treatment with a prescriber experienced in postpartum care
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: **Postpartum Mood & Anxiety Screening – Summary** | Domain | Patient‑reported Findings | |--------|----------------------------| | **Affective State** | • Persistent sadness and “heavy, down” mood reported daily (Q8).
• Low enjoyment/pleasure: rarely laughs or sees humor (Q1); limited anticipation of positive events (Q2). | | **Behavioral Indicators** | • Crying episodes 1‑2 times per week (Q9).
• Difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep; frequent night‑time awakenings with racing thoughts (Q7). | | **Cognitive/Appraisal** | • Frequent self‑blame/guilt about perceived parenting failures (Q3). | | **Anxiety/Panic** | • Ongoing, non‑situational worry about baby’s safety and performance (Q4).
• Recurrent panic‑like fear episodes with physiological arousal (heart racing) occurring “quite often” (Q5). | | **Stress/Overwhelm** | • Reports feeling “on top of” responsibilities; sense of being overwhelmed by infant care, household tasks, and exhaustion (Q6). | | **Suicidal Ideation / Safety** | • Brief, fleeting thoughts of self‑harm noted several times in the past week, without plan or intent (Q10). **Flagged as a safety concern.** | ### Consistent Patterns - **Low mood** with anhedonia (loss of laughter, reduced anticipation). - **Anxiety** that is pervasive and not clearly linked to external stressors. - **Guilt/self‑criticism** related to maternal role. - **Sleep disturbance** secondary to mood and rumination. - **Overwhelm** and perceived inability to cope with daily demands. - **Occasional self‑harm thoughts** despite lack of intent. ### Screening Significance (Postpartum Depression / Anxiety) - Core depressive symptoms: persistent sadness, anhedonia, crying, sleep disruption, guilt. - Core anxiety symptoms: excessive worry, panic‑type fear, feeling “on top of” responsibilities. - **Safety risk**: passive suicidal ideation warrants immediate safety assessment and possible crisis planning. ### Risk Flags - **Mood:** Persistent sadness, loss of pleasure, crying spells. - **Sleep:** Insomnia/fragmented sleep associated with mood disturbance. - **Cognition:** Self‑blame, feelings of inadequacy as a mother. - **Anxiety/Panic:** Frequent worry, panic episodes, sense of being overwhelmed. - **Suicidality:** Passive self‑harm thoughts – **requires prompt safety evaluation**. **Overall Impression:** The patient exhibits multiple symptoms consistent with significant postpartum depressive and anxiety symptomatology, including a safety concern for suicidal ideation. Further comprehensive assessment and immediate safety planning are indicated.
